reviews.question: Which of the following options can always be approximated to be an ideal gas?
reviews.explanation: The ideal-gas approximation neglects intermolecular forces and the volume occupied by molecules compared with the container volume. A highly superheated, sufficiently dilute vapour is therefore the intended choice (a); saturated vapour and a dense supercritical fluid are not generally ideal. Water vapour mixed with air is commonly treated as ideal when its partial pressure is sufficiently low. Steam means water in its vapour phase; it need not be at an exceptionally high temperature, and it can be approximated as ideal when the state permits. The word “always” in the question is too strong: superheat by itself does not guarantee negligible real-gas effects at arbitrary pressure.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Assumptions of ideal gas:
• Intermolecular force should be negligible.
• Volume occupied by the molecules should be negligible compared to container volume.
• Water vapour mixed with air is considered as ideal gas.
• Steam should never be considered as ideal gas unless mentioned.
• Steam is the special term given to the gaseous form of water only when present at high temperature.
reviews.note: Retained the intended best choice, with the required low-density qualification. Corrected the source’s blanket rejection of ideal steam and its restrictive definition of steam.

reviews.question: Pick the correct statement about pure substances,

options.a: A mixture of liquid air and gaseous air is a pure substances.
options.b: A mixture of ice and liquid water is not a pure substance.
options.c: A mixture of two or more phases of pure substances is not a pure substance even though the chemical composition of all the phases is the same throughout.
options.d: A mixture of two or more phases of pure substance is still a pure substance as long as the chemical composition of all the phases is the same throughout.

reviews.explanation: A pure substance has a uniform, fixed chemical composition. It may contain two or more phases provided the composition of every phase is the same throughout. Thus ice and liquid water are still one pure substance. Liquid air and gaseous air generally have different compositions during phase equilibrium and do not meet this requirement. Therefore (d) is correct.

reviews.question: Calculate the dryness fraction of steam which has 1.5 kg of water in suspension with 50 kg of steam

Hence (a).

reviews.question: An ideal gas having the weight of 20 N/m³ at the temperature of 27°C and pressure of 0.206 N/mm² (abs). The gas constant will be [Consider g = 9.81 m/s²]
reviews.explanation:
Specific weight is 20 N/m³, so density ρ = 20/9.81 kg/m³. The absolute pressure is 0.206 N/mm² = 206000 Pa and T ≈ 27 + 273 = 300 K.
From PV = mRT, or P = ρRT,
R = P/(ρT) = 206000/[(20/9.81) × 300] = 336.81 J/(kg·K) = 0.33681 kJ/(kg·K).
None of the printed choices equals this result. The source sets up the same substitution but incorrectly reports 425.1 J/(kg·K), so its key (c) cannot be verified.

reviews.question: It is desired to store 28 kg of nitrogen at 14 MPa pressure and 27°C in a_ cylinder. Assuming that nitrogen behaves like an ideal gas, determine the size of the cylinder.
reviews.explanation:
Given m = 28 kg, P = 14 MPa = 14000 kPa and T ≈ 300 K. For nitrogen, M = 28 kg/kmol and Rᵤ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K), hence R = Rᵤ/M = 8.314/28 = 0.2969 kJ/(kg·K).
Using PV = mRT,
V = mRT/P = (28 × 0.2969 × 300)/14000 = 0.178157 m³ ≈ 0.1782 m³.
Thus the cylinder volume is (b).

Ideal gas equation PV = mRT, where R = R̄/M. Molecular weight for N₂ = 28. R̄ = 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K).
R = 8.314/28 = 0.2969 kJ/(K·kg).
V = (28 × 0.2969 × 300)/(14 × 1000).
V = 0.178157 m³.

reviews.question: Which of the following law governs the isothermal process
reviews.explanation:
Boyle’s law governs an isothermal process for a fixed mass of ideal gas: T = constant and P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ = constant.
For comparison, Charles’s law applies at constant pressure, V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ = constant. Gay-Lussac’s law applies at constant volume: pressure varies directly with absolute temperature, so P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ = constant.
Therefore (a) is correct.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Boyle’s law governs the isothermal process. T = constant; P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ = constant.
Charles’s law: P = constant; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ = constant.
Gay-Lussac’s law states that pressure of a given mass of gas varies directly with absolute temperature when volume is kept constant: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ = constant.

reviews.question: According to kinetic theory of gases, the kinetic energy of translation of a molecule is proportional to

reviews.question: If a₁ and a₂ are the dryness fractions obtained in separating calorimeter and throttling calorimeter respectively, then the actual dryness fraction of steam will be:
reviews.explanation: A separating calorimeter alone assumes that all suspended water has been removed, which is not exactly true. A throttling calorimeter can determine the remaining stream’s quality only if the steam becomes superheated after throttling. In a combined apparatus, let a₁ be the fraction of the original sample that passes the separator and a₂ the vapour fraction of that remaining stream measured by throttling. The original dry-vapour mass is a₂ times the passed mass, so the actual dryness fraction is x_actual = a₁a₂, choice (d).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
The separating calorimeter when used alone does not give a very accurate result because we have to assume that all the water is separated out from the steam while passing through the calorimeter, which is not the case. Also the throttling calorimeter is only able to measure the dryness fraction of steam if the steam gets superheated after throttling.
Actual dryness fraction x_actual = a₁ × a₂.

reviews.question: The......... states that change of internal energy of a perfect gas is directly proportional to the change of temperature
reviews.explanation: Joule’s thermodynamic law states that the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature, independently of pressure and volume. Thus du = cᵥ(T)dT; for a calorically perfect gas with constant cᵥ, Δu = cᵥΔT, so the change is directly proportional to temperature change. This is the “Joule’s second law” named in the source, giving (d). The source separately calls electrical resistance heating Joule’s first law: for a conductor the generated heat is proportional to I²Rt.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Joule’s First law: a physical law expressing the relationship between the heat generated and current flowing through a conductor.
Joule’s second law: the change of internal energy of a perfect gas is directly proportional to the change of temperature and independent of its volume and pressure.

reviews.question: During melting the volume of pure substance other than water :
reviews.explanation: For most ordinary substances, the liquid is less dense than the solid, so melting increases volume and choice (b) is intended. The source’s ordinary-substance fusion curve has positive slope: dP/dT = Δh_fus/(TΔv_fus) > 0 because Δv_fus > 0. Thus liquid → solid contracts and solid → liquid expands. For water near its ordinary melting point the fusion curve has negative slope, Δv_fus < 0: ice → liquid contracts and liquid → ice expands. Water is a familiar exception, but it is not the only substance that expands on freezing; the stem is a general engineering approximation.

General substance fusion curve: (∂P/∂T)_general substance = positive. Liquid → solid: contract. Solid → liquid: expands.
H₂O fusion curve: (∂P/∂T)_H₂O = negative. Solid → liquid: contracts. Liquid → solid: expands.

reviews.question: The temperature of an ideal gas always decreases during
reviews.explanation: For an isentropic expansion of an ideal gas with positive heat capacity, ds = cᵥ dT/T + R dv/v = 0. Since dv > 0, dT < 0; for constant cᵥ this is T v^(γ−1) = constant. Adiabatic expansion alone need not lower T: in ideal-gas free expansion Q = W = 0, so Δu = 0 and T is unchanged.

reviews.question: What is the degree of freedom at critical point of water (pure substance)?
reviews.explanation:
The critical point is the endpoint where the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour lines meet and the phase distinction disappears. For a specified pure substance its critical temperature and pressure are fixed; if the state is constrained to remain exactly critical, there is no adjustable intensive variable, giving the intended answer F = 0, (c). This is a special critical-point constraint and is not obtained by treating liquid and vapour as two distinct phases in the ordinary phase rule.
For water, T_c ≈ 374°C and modern P_c ≈ 220.64 bar; the source prints 221.2 bar. The latent heat of vaporization goes to zero at the critical point. Along the ordinary liquid–vapour saturation curve, raising pressure raises the boiling temperature and the latent heat tends to decrease to zero at criticality.
The source’s region table reads: critical point—0 degrees of freedom; subcooled region—2; wet region—1; superheated region—2. In the single-phase regions two independent intensive properties specify the state; along saturation pressure and temperature are dependent. For a two-phase mixture an additional quality is required for total mixture properties.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Critical point: It is the intersection point of saturated liquid line and saturated vapour line, or a point above which the liquid directly flashes off into the vapour.
At the critical point the degree of freedom is zero.
At the critical point P + F = C + 1 (not C + 2); 2 + F = 1 + 1; F = 0.
[Critical-point T–s dome with subcooled, wet and superheated regions and x = 0 and x = 1 labels.]
At the critical point water temperature T_c = 374°C and pressure P_c = 221.2 bar.
At the critical point enthalpy of vaporisation (latent heat) will be zero.
On increasing pressure of liquid, the boiling point increases and latent heat decreases.
Degree of freedom F | Condition
0 | At critical point
2 | Subcooled region
1 | Wet region
2 | Superheated region
reviews.note: Retained the complete two-page source discussion and table as text. Corrected the misleading flash-off description, the unsupported modified phase-rule derivation and the water critical pressure.

reviews.question: In steam tables, the entropy is shown as zero for
reviews.explanation: The zero of tabulated entropy is a reference convention. Steam tables conventionally set saturated liquid water’s entropy to zero near 0°C, more precisely at the triple-point reference around 0.01°C. Thus (d) is the intended answer. This is a table datum rather than a claim that the liquid has zero absolute entropy.
reviews.sourceExplanation: In steam tables, entropy is shown as zero for a saturated liquid at 0°C ≈ 0.01°C.

reviews.question: All gases have compressibility factor of nearly unity

options.a: At very high temperatures and pressures
options.b: At very low pressures approaching zero

reviews.explanation: The compressibility factor Z = Pv/(RT) measures departure from the ideal-gas equation. For an ideal gas Z = 1. At fixed finite temperature, intermolecular interactions become negligible in the dilute limit P → 0, so every ordinary gas approaches Z = 1 in that limit. Thus (b), rather than high pressure or proximity to the critical point.
reviews.sourceExplanation: Compressibility factor Z, also known as compression factor, is a correction factor which describes deviation of a real gas from ideal gas. For ideal gas Z = 1. Z = PV/(RT). Z is nearly unity at very low pressure approaching zero.

reviews.question: Most of the gases exhibit drop in temperature upon expansion. However, this may not be true in case of
reviews.explanation: The source is discussing insulated throttling through a valve or porous plug, the Joule–Thomson (Joule–Kelvin) process, rather than every possible expansion. Its temperature response is μ_JT = (∂T/∂P)ₕ; because pressure falls, positive μ_JT produces cooling and negative μ_JT produces heating. At ordinary room temperature both hydrogen and helium typically warm on throttling, and neon is another low-inversion-temperature example. Many other gases cool. Thus both printed choices (c) and (d) satisfy the intended exception. The source itself notes that both are correct despite the official marker (c); this is not a unique one-answer item.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
In thermodynamics, the Joule–Thomson effect (also known as Joule–Kelvin or Kelvin–Joule effect) describes the temperature change of a real gas or liquid when forced through a valve or porous plug while insulated so no heat is exchanged with the environment. This procedure is called throttling or the Joule–Thomson process. At room temperature, all gases except hydrogen, helium, and neon gives heating effect upon expansion by the Joule–Thomson process when being throttled through an orifice, there are three gases experience the same effect but only at lower temperature.
Note: Option (c & d) both are correct. But official answer is (c).
reviews.note: Source explicitly acknowledges two valid options. Its sentence about gases except hydrogen, helium and neon giving heating reverses the ordinary cooling/heating distinction; corrected in the reviewed explanation.

reviews.question: If the dryness fraction of a sample by throttling calorimeter is 0.8 and that by separating calorimeter is also 0.8, then the actual dryness fraction of sample will be taken as
reviews.explanation: Let x₁ be the separator’s apparent dryness fraction and x₂ the dryness fraction of the stream entering the throttling calorimeter. In a combined separating-and-throttling measurement the original quality is x = x₁x₂. With x₁ = x₂ = 0.8, x = 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64, choice (c).
reviews.sourceExplanation:
x₁ = dryness fraction of steam considering separating calorimeter.
x₂ = dryness fraction of steam entering the throttling calorimeter.
x = x₁x₂.
Actual dryness fraction of steam in the sample x = 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.64.

reviews.question: The value of dryness fraction at critical point for water-steam phase transformation may be
reviews.explanation: Quality or dryness fraction is defined only when distinct saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour masses can be identified: x = m_v/(m_l + m_v). At the critical point liquid and vapour become indistinguishable, so quality is undefined; equivalently the two-phase property formula x = (v − v_f)/(v_g − v_f) has a zero denominator. The source explanation correctly says “undefined,” but none of the printed options states this. “All of these” does not make the numerical values 0 and 1 valid at criticality. No unique answer can be checked.
reviews.sourceExplanation: The value of dryness fraction at critical point for water–steam phase transformation is undefined.
reviews.note: The printed key (d) contradicts the complete adjacent explanation. Preserved the choices and source key; undefined is absent from the options.

reviews.question: A Saturation state of pure substance (water) is a:

options.a: State from which a change of phase may occur with a change in pressure or temperature.
options.b: State from which a change of phase may occur with a change in pressure and temperature.
options.c: State from which a change of phase may occur with a change in pressure and volume.
options.d: State from which a change of phase may occur without a change in pressure and temperature.
options.e: State from which a change of phase may occur without a change in pressure or temperature.

reviews.explanation: At a saturated state a pure substance can change between liquid and vapour while pressure and temperature remain at their paired saturation values. The source T–s dome shows a horizontal constant-P, constant-T phase-change line joining the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapour boundaries. This is the intended meaning of (d). However, (e), “without a change in pressure or temperature,” has the same ordinary meaning of neither variable changing. The two printed alternatives are effectively duplicates, so the item has no unique one-answer key.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Saturation state: A saturation state of pure substance (water) is a state from which a change of phase may occur without a change in pressure and temperature.
[T–s diagram with critical point, constant P and constant T line, saturated-liquid line and saturated-vapour line.]
reviews.note: Both (d) and (e) describe unchanged pressure and temperature. Source marker (d) retained; duplicate valid alternatives prevent automatic grading.

reviews.question: Universal gas constant is defined as equal to product of the molecular weight of the gas and
reviews.explanation: For an ideal gas PV = nRᵤT = mRT. Since n = m/M, comparison gives Rᵤ = MR. Thus the universal (molar) gas constant is the product of molecular/molar mass and specific or characteristic gas constant, choice (d). Rᵤ ≈ 8.314 kJ/(kmol·K).
reviews.sourceExplanation: Ideal gas equation PV = nRT. The universal gas constant or molar constant Rᵤ is the product of specific gas constant R and molecular mass M. Rᵤ = MR, Rᵤ = 8.314 kJ/(kg-mol·K).

reviews.question: Consider the following statements for a throttling process. 1. It is an adiabatic process 2. There is no work transfer in the process 3. Entropy increases in throttling process Which of these statements are correct?
reviews.explanation: An ordinary throttling device is modeled as a steady adiabatic flow with no shaft work. Neglecting kinetic and potential energy changes, the steady-flow energy equation then gives h₁ = h₂. A finite pressure drop through the restriction is irreversible; with Q = 0 the entropy balance gives s₂ − s₁ = s_gen > 0. Thus all three statements are correct, (a). Entropy increases because of internal irreversibility, not because heat is transferred through the insulated device.
reviews.sourceExplanation: Throttling process is an adiabatic process and has no work transfer in the process and entropy increases in this due to heat transfer.
reviews.note: The answer is correct but the source incorrectly attributes entropy production to heat transfer while calling the process adiabatic.

reviews.question: The process of superheating follows :
reviews.explanation: The intended model is constant-pressure heating of sufficiently dilute superheated vapour. Charles’s law then follows from PV = mRT: V/T = constant at fixed P and mass, so V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂. This gives intended choice (c). Superheating is not intrinsically governed by Charles’s law at arbitrary pressure or for nonideal steam; the constant-pressure ideal-gas approximation is required.
reviews.sourceExplanation: The process of superheating follows Charles’s law. According to Charles’s law P = constant; V/T = constant; V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂.
reviews.note: Restored the full equations and supplied the pressure and ideal-gas assumptions missing from the blanket source claim.

reviews.question: Ideal gas equation may be written as [where, P = absolute pressure, v = specific volume, R = characteristic gas constant, T = absolute temperature, m = mass of gas, n = number of moles of gas, Z = compressibility factor]:
reviews.explanation: For specific volume v = V/m and the characteristic gas constant R, the ideal-gas equation is Pv = RT, choice (d). More generally Z = Pv/(RT), so an ideal gas has Z = 1. PV = mRT uses total volume, while PV = nRᵤT uses the universal molar constant. The real-gas expression Pv = ZRT in (b) also reduces to (d) if Z = 1; (d) is the canonical ideal-gas equation requested with these symbols.
reviews.sourceExplanation: Compressibility factor Z = Pv/(RT). For ideal gas Z = 1. Then Pv = RT.

reviews.question: Generalized compressibility chart is drawn between:

options.a: Reduced pressure (P,) on y-axis and reduced temperature (T,) on x-axis
options.b: Compressibility factor (Z) on y-axis and reduced temperature (T;) on x-axis
options.c: Compressibility factor (Z) on y-axis and reduced pressure (P,) on x-axis
options.d: Compressibility factor (Z) on x-axis and reduced pressure (P,) on y-axis

reviews.explanation:
A generalized compressibility chart plots compressibility factor Z on the vertical axis against reduced pressure P_r = P/P_c on the horizontal axis, with curves for reduced temperature T_r = T/T_c. Thus (c).
Z = P v_actual/(RT) = v_actual/v_ideal at the same pressure and temperature. Z = 1 represents the ideal-gas value; Z > 1 means a larger volume than the ideal value and Z < 1 a smaller volume. The source describes these as “less compressible” and “more compressible,” respectively, but Z itself is not the derivative compressibility coefficient.
reviews.sourceExplanation:
Generalized compressibility chart is drawn between compressibility factor Z on y-axis and reduced pressure P_r on x-axis.
[Compressibility chart: Z against P_r, curves labeled T_r > T′_r.]
Z = P v_actual/(RT) = v_actual/v_ideal.
Z = 1: for ideal gas.
Z > 1: less compressible.
Z < 1: more compressible.
reviews.note: Retained the complete source definition and chart; clarified that Z compares volumes and is not itself isothermal compressibility.
